items.title: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
items.summary: I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it. Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories. But... sometimes that uv.lock pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today: error: Failed to build `watchfiles==1.1.1` cause: Call to `maturin.build_wheel` failed error: the configured Python interpreter version (3.15) is newer than PyO3's maximum supported version (3.14) Deleting that file and running uv run pytest again usually fixes the problem. items.title: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
items.summary: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews ), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe. It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data. Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard , which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe. That message receiving code uses innerHTML , so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method. This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions. OpenAI’s CSP rules blocked inline scripts entirely, and only allowed script loading from a handful of domains, but one of those was YouTube - and the YouTube oEmbed endpoint could be used to reflect JavaScript back in a way that executed it. Once the attack had JavaScript execution on ChatGPT, it was trivial to fetch private user data from APIs and exfiltrate it via an image reference. The end result: you could create a ChatGPT share URL which, when visited by another signed-in user, could exfiltrate their private data or take actions on their behalf. items.title: dbreunig/nesformer
items.summary: dbreunig/nesformer Inspired by qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B. You can now play NES ROMs such as Super Mario Bros (very slowly) running inside Qwen! In a comment on Hacker News Drew reveals the Opus 5.5 prompts he used to build this system: Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed. Followed by: I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM. Apparently Opus found and then used this collection of conformance tests for the NES CPU released 15 years ago by Christopher Pow. items.title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
items.summary: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. This is continuous deployment turned up to 11: A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [.

items.summary: In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered: Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra [ ... ] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7. — Ted Sanders , explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions Tags: generative-ai , gpt , openai , ai , llms , ted-sanders

items.summary: GitHub Octoverse 2026 I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular: This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month. The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location . Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...] Industry . Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...] Interoperability . Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation. items.title: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox
items.summary: Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox webframe is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a web page like a program" - you point it at a URL or file and it executes it in a hidden headless web view and outputs console.log() to standard output and any exceptions to standard error. It's written in Go on top of the glaze library, which provides access to a system browser ("WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows") so it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine. It reminds me of my own shot-scraper javascript tool, albeit in a much smaller package that doesn't depend on Playwright. I had Claude Opus 5.5 put it through its paces and prepare a research report for me. items.title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
items.summary: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier. I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August: llm openai endpoint \ https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \ --key kimi \ -m kimi-k3.1-pro \ "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \ --responses \ -o reasoning_effort low \ > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \ 2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace). Here are the pelicans I got for Kimi K3.1 Pro on the three reasoning levels it supports - low, medium, and max. This is max: For comparison, I ran fresh pelicans against Kimi K3 on those three reasoning levels. it.title: Airbnb e il 'cervello aziendale' per gli agenti IA

it.extended_analysis:
Gli agenti IA dipendono spesso dalla conoscenza tacita che i dipendenti esperti accumulano nel tempo, la quale raramente entra a far parte della documentazione ufficiale. Airbnb sta affrontando questa sfida con Project Everest, un'infrastruttura pensata per raccogliere e organizzare tale sapere aziendale.

Durante la conversazione, vengono esaminati i rischi derivanti da informazioni obsolete e dal fenomeno del 'context poisoning', in cui una quantità eccessiva o scorretta di dati può compromettere le prestazioni dei sistemi intelligenti. Vengono inoltre analizzati i metodi per valutare l'impatto reale del lavoro ingegneristico e le limitazioni delle interfacce basate su chat.
it.context: Nel panorama tecnologico attuale, le aziende cercano di andare oltre i semplici assistenti conversazionali, puntando su agenti autonomi capaci di integrarsi nei processi operativi quotidiani e di mediare in scenari complessi.
key_takeaways: Project Everest raccoglie la conoscenza aziendale nascosta nei flussi di lavoro per gli agenti IA.
Il 'context poisoning' e la gestione di informazioni obsolete rappresentano ostacoli significativi.

items.title: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise
items.summary: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise This is very, very bad news: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores. Any software that bundles a list of trusted certificates needs to be updated. This site is tracking software updates via this GitHub repository - Linux distros need to update their ca-certificates packages. In Python world uv 0.13.4 and pip 26.2.2 and certifi 2026.10.19 have been released with upgraded certificate lists. There's a very informative thread about this on the official Python forum. Por último, se debaten los compromisos entre los ingresos por publicidad y orgánicos, el perfeccionamiento continuo y el delicado límite entre la personalización útil y la vigilancia.

Elección de Rust en el backend para lograr una infraestructura de ranking dinámica de baja latencia.
Evaluación de la línea divisoria entre la personalización comercial útil y la vigilancia.

it.title: SIREN: Un indice orario e verificabile sull'attività dell'IA
it.summary: È stato rilasciato SIREN (precedentemente noto come DOOMCON), un indice orario dell'attività dell'IA progettato per essere verificabile. Sviluppato in JavaScript e ospitato su GitHub, il progetto utilizza ricevute concatenate da funzioni di hash con un metodo aperto.
it.why_it_matters: Offrire un sistema di tracciamento trasparente e verificabile dell'attività dell'intelligenza artificiale è cruciale per monitorare il settore senza ricorrere a pubblicità o tracciamenti.
it.extended_analysis:
Il progetto, descritto come un indice orario dell'attività dell'intelligenza artificiale, punta sulla trasparenza grazie all'impiego di ricevute concatenate tramite hash e a una metodologia aperta. Senza sponsorizzazioni pubblicitarie o sistemi di tracciamento degli utenti, la piattaforma si posiziona come uno strumento indipendente per osservare i flussi di dati e le dinamiche del settore.

Nel contesto attuale, in cui la misurazione dell'evoluzione dell'IA è spesso opaca o legata a metriche commerciali, iniziative basate su registri verificabili offrono un approccio alternativo. Sarà importante osservare come evolverà l'adozione di questo indice e quali metriche specifiche verranno integrate nel tempo.
it.context: Il monitoraggio indipendente dello sviluppo dell'intelligenza artificiale è un tema centrale per ricercatori e sviluppatori che cercano standard aperti e verificabili per analizzare i progressi tecnologici.
key_takeaways: SIREN fornisce un indice orario dell'attività dell'IA.
Il sistema utilizza ricevute concatenate e un metodo aperto.
Il codice è scritto in JavaScript ed è disponibile su GitHub senza pubblicità o tracciamento.

As the industry grows, reliable and transparent ways to measure AI activity remain in high demand. Watching how this open methodology develops will show whether verifiable hash-chained indices can become a standard tool for independent observers.

es.title: SIREN: Un índice horario y verificable de la actividad de IA
es.summary: Se ha lanzado SIREN (antes conocido como DOOMCON), un índice horario de la actividad de la inteligencia artificial diseñado para ser verificable. Desarrollado en JavaScript en GitHub, utiliza recibos encadenados por hash y un método abierto sin anuncios ni rastreo.
es.why_it_matters: Contar con un sistema de seguimiento transparente y verificable de la actividad de la IA es fundamental para supervisar el sector de forma independiente.

El proyecto ofrece un registro horario basado en recibos con cadenas de hash y una metodología abierta. Al prescindir por completo de publicidad y herramientas de rastreo, busca garantizar la integridad y la independencia en la observación de la actividad tecnológica.

En un entorno donde la medición del avance de la IA suele ser compleja y poco transparente, las soluciones abiertas basadas en criptografía ligera ofrecen nuevas vías de análisis. Habrá que seguir de evolución técnica del proyecto en GitHub.
es.context: La demanda de metodologías abiertas y verificables para auditar el ecosistema de la inteligencia artificial impulsa el desarrollo de herramientas independientes.
key_takeaways: SIREN proporciona un índice horario de la actividad de la IA.

No incluye publicidad ni sistemas de seguimiento.

Small delays, awkward interruptions, or the wrong tone can quickly break the illusion—and adding vision and visual presence only raises the stakes. In this episode, Alex Smola, co-founder and CEO of Boson AI, explores the path from today’s voice agents to audiovisual agents and AI avatars. We discuss the technical tradeoffs behind real-time voice, including audio tokenization, latency, model size, and inference cost, as well as what changes when these systems can both see and be seen. We also explore the role of emotional intelligence in AI, how agents can learn from human interactions, and what it will take to move beyond impressive demos toward interactions that actually feel natural. 🗒️ Full show notes: https://twimlai.com/go/777.

Do AI Tokenomics Matter More Than Model Benchmarks? with Chris Potts - #776
items.summary: As reasoning models consume more tokens and AI systems become more expensive to run, understanding what those tokens actually buy is becoming increasingly important. In this episode, Stanford professor and Big Spin co-founder Chris Potts joins us to discuss AI tokenomics and his research into “tokenflation”—the possibility that token usage is growing faster than the measurable value those tokens produce. We explore how to measure the return on AI spending, why benchmarks alone provide an incomplete picture of model progress, and what inference-time scaling means for the economics of increasingly capable models. Chris also explains why expert AI users tend to get better results by challenging and iterating with models, how AI fluency affects outcomes, and why more efficient architectures could change the underlying economics. We also discuss DSPy, interpretability, the limits of today’s transformer architectures, and where Chris sees opportunities for more fundamental innovation in AI. 🗒️ Full show notes: ⁠⁠https://twimlai.com/go/776.

items.title: Why the Next AI Breakthrough May Come from Physics with Max Welling - #774
items.summary: The conventional wisdom in AI is that the next breakthrough will come from more compute, more data, and larger models. But what if the next leap comes from somewhere else? In this episode, Max Welling—co-founder and CTO of CuspAI and professor at the University of Amsterdam—argues that physics may provide some of the ideas behind the next generation of AI systems. We begin with CuspAI’s work using generative AI to design entirely new materials for semiconductors, batteries, carbon capture, and clean energy. Max explains how foundation models for chemistry, agentic workflows, simulation, and automated experimentation are dramatically accelerating the search for new materials and reshaping scientific discovery. The conversation then broadens into a deeper question. Beyond giving AI new scientific problems to solve, can physics also teach us how to build better AI? Max explores surprising connections between machine learning and thermodynamics, why waves may become a new computational primitive for neural networks, and how concepts like symmetry breaking and statistical physics could inspire AI architectures beyond today’s scaling paradigm. 🗒️ Full show notes: https://twimlai.com/go/774.

items.summary: Text-to-image models have become remarkably good at producing realistic images. But realism isn’t the same as correctness. We explore why better training objectives can improve controllability, how separating scene planning from rendering may lead to more reliable image generation, techniques for generating 16-megapixel images efficiently on edge devices, and new methods for eliminating the visible artifacts that often appear in AI-powered image editing. Along the way, we discuss reinforcement learning for image generation, agentic image generation pipelines, on-device AI, and what the next phase of progress in generative vision systems is likely to look like. 🗒️ Full show notes: https://twimlai.com/go/773

Why Models Are AI’s Next Training Dataset with Damian Borth - #772
items.summary: For more than a decade, AI has advanced by training ever-larger models on ever-larger datasets. But as high-quality training data becomes harder to find and pretraining grows increasingly expensive, researchers are looking for new ways to keep foundation models improving. In this episode, Damian Borth, professor of AI and machine learning at the University of St. Gallen, argues we’ve been overlooking an important source of knowledge: the models we’ve already trained. His group’s work on weight space learning treats trained neural networks themselves as data, learning from the distilled results of millions of GPU hours of optimization rather than starting from raw data each time. We explore what it means to build foundation models of neural networks, how knowledge can be transferred across architectures and domains, why this approach could dramatically reduce the cost of developing specialized models, and whether future AI systems may be trained on collections of existing models instead of ever-growing datasets. 🗒️ Full show notes: https://twimlai.com/go/772.
